title: Ofcom on the Online Safety Act: Progress, Enforcement and Reform
label: 15 Sep 2026 · Ofcom evidence
summary: Ofcom officials updated the committee on implementing the Online Safety Act, reporting progress on age checks and risk assessments but acknowledging underwhelming results on children's safety. They discussed enforcement powers, delays, legal challenges, and suggested reforms to the safe harbour and business disruption measures.

speakers.label: Committee Member
speakers.name: Committee Member
speakers.role: Combines repetitive questions from various committee members

speakers.label: Mark Bunting
speakers.name: Mark Bunting
speakers.role: Director, Online Safety Strategy Delivery, Ofcom

chapters.title: Implementation Status
chapters.takeaway: Most Online Safety Act duties are in force, with categorised services expected by mid-2027, but new social media bans may require extra funding and sequencing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Could you outline which parts of the Online Safety Act are now active and what's still pending?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We're balancing implementation, compliance, and new duties like the social media ban. Mark can detail the timeline.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: Illegal harms and children's protection duties have been in force since early 2025. Categorised services were delayed by a judicial review but should be fully operational by mid-2027.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We're also implementing new offences from the Crime and Policing Act and consulting on a 48-hour takedown duty for intimate images.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about the impact of the Government's social media ban for under-16s on your timetable?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We were already fully loaded, so we've moved staff to the ban work. The Government has promised extra funding, and we're in detailed discussions to sequence everything. It's doable with the right resources.

chapters.title: Lessons Learned and Engagement
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom learned to engage more collaboratively with industry and civil society, but the safe harbour provision limits enforcement flexibility.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What lessons have you learned from implementing the first phases, and how are they shaping the next category 1 duties?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We've learned to engage more with stakeholders. For example, our work on women and girls was collaborative, and we're doing the same for transparency reports. But the safe harbour means if companies follow our codes, they're deemed compliant even if risks remain.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The Children's Commissioner said you wouldn't share risk assessments with her. Why?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We haven't received a formal request. Under Section 393, we need company consent to share. If she formally asks, we'll liaise with companies to see if they agree.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So if she makes a formal request, you'll facilitate?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Yes, we'll follow the process and check with the companies.

chapters.title: Impact on Safety
chapters.takeaway: Age checks have increased and some services have improved, but overall impact on children's safety is still underwhelming, with AI supercharging harms.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Has the Act made people safer online?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We've seen big changes: 76% of companies completed risk assessments, and age checks have surged, especially on porn sites. But we're underwhelmed by the overall effect so far, especially on big services used by children.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The Children's Commissioner said the Act has made 'absolutely no difference'. How do you respond?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We share the frustration. This is about changing corporate culture, which takes time. We're at an early point, but we're driving change.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We've seen steps, like commitments from X, Meta, and Snap, but there's a long way to go. For example, they need better ways to identify child users to make systems work.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Should tech companies be allowed to operate if they can't guarantee children's safety?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Society says no. The Act puts duties on companies, and we can enforce, including business disruption measures that block UK access if they don't comply.

chapters.title: Gaming and Proactive Tech
chapters.takeaway: Gaming has seen some age gates and controls, but Ofcom's focus is narrow; proactive monitoring tools are key but require overcoming legal thresholds.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What progress in gaming?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Services like Xbox and Steam have introduced age gates, but it's not our top priority. Social media and children's protection come first.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We've focused on user interactions, like on Roblox, where age verification and controls have been effective. But broader issues like violence and screen time aren't covered by the Act.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The Molly Rose Foundation says exposure to harmful content hasn't changed. What's stopping you?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We need proactive monitoring tools, but the Act requires us to prove they're accurate and effective before mandating them. We're consulting on this and will say more in autumn.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Isn't that a fundamental flaw?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: It's a tension between privacy and safety. We think the case for tools is strong, and we're working on proposals.

chapters.title: Enforcement Challenges
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom has opened many investigations and imposed fines, but legal challenges, overseas services, and non-payment hinder enforcement.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Stakeholders say Ofcom is slow and reactive. Why?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We move quickly when needed, like with Grok. But the Act covers 100,000 services, so we must prioritise. We face judicial reviews and appeals, which slow us down.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Do you have enough powers?

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: We're using our teeth. We've opened six enforcement programmes and 40 investigations, imposing £7 million in fines. But many services are overseas with no UK assets, making penalties hard to collect.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: Business disruption measures are tough because we can only apply them for ongoing non-compliance. If a service withdraws from the UK, we lose jurisdiction.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: How much of the £7 million has been paid?

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: I don't have the figure, but the majority hasn't been paid. We'll follow up.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: As we fine bigger companies with UK assets, this will become less of an issue.

chapters.title: VPNs and International Comparisons
chapters.takeaway: VPN use to evade age checks is a concern but not widespread; Ofcom can't require providers to block VPNs without legislative change.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Should the Act be amended to force companies to deal with VPNs?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: VPN use increased but not massively. This is a political decision for Government. We'll do what we're told.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The Minister said providers must account for VPNs in age assurance. Do you agree?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: They don't need to prevent VPN use. We've acted against firms encouraging VPNs, but requiring blocks would be a significant intervention needing debate.

chapters.title: Reform Suggestions
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom suggests targeted reforms: a duty to mitigate all risks, better business disruption measures, and easier use of proactive tech.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Would you support removing the safe harbour?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: It's complicated. Safe harbour gives legal certainty but limits our ability to enforce broader risk mitigation. A duty to mitigate all risks would help, but enforcement would be challenging.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What about a duty of care?

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: It's an alternative, but we'd face similar challenges in defining parameters. Safe harbour lets big services argue they're compliant even if harms persist.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: If you could change one thing, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: Empower us to pressure companies to address all identified risks, linked to a duty of care.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: Fix business disruption measures to make them more practical.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Make it easier to mandate proactive technology to control content served to users.
